# The HOA Board Will Now Come to Order

## I.

The letter was on the kitchen counter next to a foil-wrapped slice of banana bread.

Meredith Chen picked it up, read it, set it down, and read it again.

*Dear Mr. and Mrs. Chen,* it began, and then the language shifted into something she had to read twice to believe was directed at a house where a man was dying:

*This letter is to inform you that the structure recently installed on the front elevation of your property at 414 Larkspur Lane constitutes an unauthorized structural modification in violation of Article 14, Section 3(b) of the Hollow Creek Estates Covenants, Conditions & Restrictions (amended 2019). Specifically, the wooden ramp affixed to the front porch was constructed and installed without prior submission of an Architectural Modification Request (Form AMR-7), without review by the Architectural Control Committee, and without written approval from the Board of Directors.*

*In accordance with Article 18, Section 2(a), a fine of $50.00 per day will accrue beginning on the date of this notice until such time as the modification is either (a) removed or (b) retroactively approved through the standard review process, which carries an estimated timeline of 60–90 days.*

*We value you as members of our community and understand that circumstances may have created a sense of urgency. Please don't hesitate to reach out if you have questions about the review process. I'm always happy to help.*

*As always, your neighbor,*
*Doug*

From the dining room—which had not been a dining room since October, when the medical supply company hauled the table into the garage and replaced it with a hospital bed, an IV pole, and a portable oxygen concentrator—came the thin, arhythmic sound of Walter's breathing punctuated by the concentrator's metronomic hiss. A cough. A long pause in which Meredith's hand tightened on the letter. Then breathing again.

The banana bread was still warm. She could smell it through the foil—overripe banana and brown sugar—mixed with the antiseptic tang that had colonized the house so gradually she only noticed it now when she came in from outside. Someone had tied a small ribbon around the foil. Yellow.

Fifty dollars a day. She stood at the counter and did what she had done professionally for thirty-one years at Pacific Mutual: she calculated. Sixty to ninety days for retroactive approval, which meant three thousand dollars minimum, forty-five hundred if they slow-walked it, which they would, because the they was Doug, and the process was Doug, and the committee was Doug. If she removed the ramp, Walter could not leave the house. If Walter could not leave the house, he could not reach the medical transport van that took him to oncology on Tuesdays. If he could not reach oncology, the port in his chest was decorative. If the port was decorative, she was managing terminal liver cancer with encouraging words and the pamphlets the hospice nurse left on the table that was now in the garage.

She did not go to Walter. She stood in the kitchen with the letter flat on the counter under both palms, and she was not angry, not yet, not in any way that had a name she would reach for. She was running numbers. She was calculating exposure, liability, and timeline. She was identifying the risk and the risk was Doug Whitmore and his four-color-highlighted copy of the CC&Rs and his warm banana bread and his handwritten signature that looped on the D as though he were signing a birthday card.

The oxygen concentrator hissed. Walter coughed.

Meredith folded the letter precisely along its original creases, slid it back into its envelope, and placed it in the kitchen drawer where she kept insurance documents, medical power of attorney forms, and the folder labeled, in her clean actuary's print, WALTER — FINAL.

She did not touch the banana bread.

---

## II.

She went to Gloria first, on a Tuesday morning, five days after the letter.

Gloria Paik was two doors down at 410 Larkspur, on her knees in the front garden, deadheading roses with a pair of shears that looked surgical. She was sixty-six years old and had the posture of a woman who had spent three decades sitting upright in courtrooms transcribing every word anyone said, which she had.

"Gloria."

"Meredith." Gloria did not look up. She made a final cut, set the dead bloom in a neat pile with the others, and stripped off her gardening gloves. "I heard about the letter. Carla Johannsen told Peggy Webb, who told me at the mailboxes yesterday. I have it filed under both 'Chen' and 'Enforcement Actions, 2024.'"

"You file neighborhood gossip."

"I organize verbal records by date, speaker, and subject household, cross-referenced where relevant." Gloria said this with the same tone a surgeon might use to describe handwashing. "I was a court stenographer for thirty-one years. Speech that goes unrecorded might as well not have happened."

Meredith sat down on Gloria's porch step without being invited. "You were removed from that position."

Gloria's mouth thinned, which was the closest Gloria came to any recognizable display of emotion. "I was removed because during a custody proceeding in which one parent's documented history of—" She stopped. Started again. "I inserted three editorial annotations into an official court transcript. The judge's characterization of the father as 'a concerned parent' became 'a concerned parent [see attached incident reports, disregarded by this court].' I was aware that this was outside the scope of my role. I was also aware that Tyler Marcos was seven years old and had been to the emergency room four times in eight months." She picked up her shears. "It cost me my certification, my pension, and eleven months of sleep. I would do it again before lunch."

"I need your files," Meredith said.

"Which household?"

"All of them."

Gloria studied her for a moment with the particular gaze of a woman who had spent decades watching people testify and had developed, against her will, an involuntary taxonomy of human intention. Whatever she found in Meredith's face appeared to satisfy her.

"I'll bring them over Thursday," she said. "They're in binders. There are nine."

---

Leonard Bock required a different approach, mostly because Leonard Bock was not at home. He was at the Sutter County Planning Commission's monthly public hearing on a zoning variance request for a mixed-use development on Ortega Road, which had nothing to do with Hollow Creek Estates and everything to do with the fact that Leonard attended every public meeting in the county the way other men his age attended Giants games.

Meredith found him in the third row of the county building's fluorescent-lit meeting room, annotating a printed copy of the agenda with a mechanical pencil. He was seventy-one. He wore a checked short-sleeve shirt buttoned to the collar. On the folding chair beside him, stacked with the care others reserved for infant children, sat two editions of *Robert's Rules of Order Newly Revised*—the 11th and 12th—both bristling with color-coded page markers.

"Leonard."

"Meredith, sit down, this is remarkable—they're about to move to extend public comment without a proper motion to amend the agenda. It's technically a breach but I don't think anyone on the dais has the parliamentary literacy to—oh, there it is. No second. No *second*, Meredith. Do you see?"

"I need your help with something."

"Of course. After the vote on item four. They've miscounted the abstentions twice already tonight and I want to be here if it happens a third time."

She waited. Leonard watched the hearing with the rapt absorption she had only ever seen on the faces of people who had found the one thing in the world they were built to do: her husband with a spreadsheet, her daughter with a cello, Leonard Bock with a municipal agenda and a pencil worn to a stub. When item four was concluded (the abstentions were not miscounted a third time, which seemed to disappoint him), he turned to her with the full and eager attention of a retriever hearing the word "walk."

She told him about the letter, the fine, the ramp, and the 247-page document she had downloaded from the HOA's outdated website.

Leonard removed his reading glasses, closed his eyes, and pressed the bridge of his nose with two fingers.

"Two hundred and forty-seven pages," he said, "last revised 2006 with piecemeal amendments, you said?"

"Seventeen amendments. I counted."

"Reconciled?"

"I doubt it."

Leonard Bock opened his eyes, and what Meredith saw in them was not outrage on her behalf or sympathy for her situation. What she saw was the light of a man who had just been handed a 247-page procedural document riddled with internal contradictions and asked to *do something about it*. It was joy. It was nearly indecent.

"I'll need a clean copy," he said. "And a large table."

"My kitchen table is available. The dining room is occupied."

He nodded—he knew about Walter, everyone knew about Walter, it was the kind of neighborhood where everyone knew—and began packing his annotated agendas into a leather briefcase that had been old when Reagan was president.

"Meredith," he said, halfway to the door. "Has anyone ever formally challenged the chair on a procedural question at one of the annual meetings?"

"No."

"No," he repeated, softly, in the voice of a man who has just found the murder weapon. "No, they wouldn't have."

---

The Thursday-night book club met at Janet Cavanaugh's house, which smelled of pinot grigio and the rosemary candle Janet believed disguised the pinot grigio. There were six of them: Janet (sixty-two, retired school principal), Diane Okafor (fifty-eight, adjunct history professor, currently between semesters and between marriages), Bev Horner (seventy-four, the only one who still drove at night and therefore indispensable), Ruthie Marcus (sixty-three, forensic accountant, technically still working but only because she enjoyed it), Pat Sugimoto (sixty-nine, no distinguishing professional background but a reading velocity that bordered on the clinical), and Sue Pollard (sixty-seven, who had once served on the city council for a single term and described the experience as "formative in the way that dysentery is formative").

They were halfway through a book about the Medici banking family. The discussion had been vigorous. Diane had used the phrase "structural inevitability" twice, and Ruthie had pulled up actual Florentine ledger reproductions on her iPad.

Meredith accepted a glass of wine and said: "I need help with something that isn't a book."

She told them. She told them about the letter, about the fine, about the ramp Walter needed to get to the van that took him to the treatments that were, if she was being honest, no longer treatments so much as gestures of institutional optimism against a body that had made its decision. She told them about Leonard and Gloria and the 247 pages. She told them what she intended to do, which was to remove Doug Whitmore from the board at the annual meeting through a recall motion supported by documented evidence of procedural and financial misconduct.

She had expected questions, objections, perhaps the gentle reluctance the genre seemed to require.

"Oh, *finally*," said Bev.

"I've been waiting for someone to do something about that man for six years," said Pat.

"Seven," said Janet.

"Who's handling the financial audit?" asked Ruthie, already opening a blank spreadsheet on her iPad. "Because if it's that bookkeeper he uses—Karen? Karen—she's been attending my church and I can tell you that woman is holding on to something she wants to put down."

Diane, who had just finished a seven-hundred-page biography of Robespierre and was still, Meredith suspected, living inside it a little, set down her wine glass with a care that suggested she was about to say something she had been thinking for a while.

"The question isn't whether Doug should be removed," Diane said. "That's been structurally necessary for years. The question is what replaces him, and whether you've thought about the architecture of what comes after."

Nobody blinked at "structurally necessary." Nobody asked Diane to clarify that she was speaking metaphorically. Meredith, who had spent her professional life identifying risks others preferred not to name, felt a small cold recognition move through her: these women had been waiting for a project. Not a book to discuss. A project.

"I've thought about what comes after," Meredith said. "What comes after is a board that doesn't fine a dying man for the ramp that gets him to his doctor."

The room was quiet for a moment, and in the quiet Meredith heard what she always heard now: the phantom hiss of the oxygen concentrator, even when she was not home, a sound that had colonized her inner ear the way the antiseptic had colonized the house. She took a sip of wine. It tasted like wine. She had stopped tasting things precisely sometime in November.

"Well," said Sue Pollard, who had survived the city council. "Let's get to work."

---

## III.

Leonard arrived at Meredith's kitchen at eight the next morning with two annotated copies of Robert's Rules, a mechanical pencil, a fresh legal pad, and an expression of barely contained liturgical anticipation.

The CC&Rs were printed out and laid across the kitchen table—all 247 pages, including the seventeen amendments, each in its own labeled section. Gloria had already been by at seven-thirty to deliver her nine binders and a terse note: *Filed chronologically and by subject. Pink tabs are financial. Blue tabs are enforcement. Yellow tabs are personal observations. Disregard yellow tabs if preferred. I would not.*

From the next room came the concentrator's hiss. A long breath. A pause. Another long breath. The metronome of what was left.

Leonard sat down, uncapped his pencil, and began to read.

He read the way a monk reads scripture: line by line, word by word, testing each clause against the ones that preceded it and the ones that would follow. He read Articles 1 through 6 silently. At Article 7, Section 2(c)—a provision about fence height that had been amended in 2011 and then contradicted by Amendment 14 in 2018—he made a small sound, a kind of tch, as though he had found a stain on a vestment.

"He didn't reconcile," Leonard murmured. "He amended Section 2(c) without updating the reference in Article 12, which still cites the original language."

"What does that mean?" Meredith asked.

"It means either the fence provision or the landscaping setback provision is enforceable, but not both. He's been enforcing both." Leonard made a note. Then a second note. Then he turned back to Article 3 and made a third note.

Over the next five days, across four sessions at Meredith's kitchen table, Leonard mapped the entire procedural architecture of Hollow Creek Estates with the meticulous devotion of a medieval cartographer charting a coastline. Gloria sat across from him, transcribing his findings into a clean document as he dictated, her fingers moving with the eerie speed of a woman whose hands had spent three decades keeping up with human speech. Meredith moved between the kitchen and Walter's room, bringing water, adjusting the bed, checking the oxygen, returning to the table to ask questions Leonard did not always answer because he was deep inside a subordinate clause and could not be reached.

The findings accumulated:

The quorum requirement for the annual meeting was defined in Article 9, Section 1 as "a majority of members in good standing." But Amendment 11, passed in 2017, had redefined "good standing" to exclude members with unpaid fines—and Doug, as sole arbiter of fines, could theoretically shrink the eligible voting pool to guarantee any outcome he wanted.
